primary_text_note: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/silas-marner.txt is Gutenberg #26269, a LibriVox AUDIOBOOK catalogue - it contains no prose, only chapter timings, so no quotation could be checked against it. Every quotation was checked against Gutenberg #550 (the actual Silas Marner text, 429 KB), fetched to the scratchpad for this run. Recommend repointing the brief for this unit.

findings.claim: "For Edexcel 1ET0 Component 2, Section A ... Part (a) ... (AO1 + AO2). Part (b) ... (AO1 + AO2)." Lesson 7 repeats it: the extract task rewards "AO1 + AO2" and the wider-text task "also AO1 + AO2".
findings.truth: On the 19th-century novel question part (a) is marked for AO2 alone and part (b) for AO1 alone, 20 marks each. Telling students both parts reward both objectives sends them into part (b) doing language analysis instead of building a critical, personal argument. The strings "Edexcel 1ET0" and "Component 2, Section A" are also banned house strings.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md L1161-1170 (Section A two-part question, AOs covered are AO1 and AO2) and the AO grid L1337-1360 (Questions 1a-7a = 20 AO2; Questions 1b-7b = 20 AO1); brief verified facts.

findings.claim: "Context is not separately assessed on the Edexcel paper" (lesson 1) and "Context is not a separate AO in this paper" (lesson 7).
findings.truth: True of the novel question only. On the same paper the named-poem comparison is explicitly assessed for the contexts in which the poems were written (AO3). A student could conclude that context never earns marks on Paper 2.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md L1171-1178: Section B Part 1 questions focus on language, form, structure (AO2) and the contexts in which the poems were written (AO3).

findings.claim: "he lives in a northern industrial town called Lantern Yard"; flashcard stem "What northern town does Silas come from before Raveloe?" keyed to "Lantern Yard."
findings.truth: Lantern Yard is a narrow alley and its chapel inside a large manufacturing town that Eliot never names. Silas himself calls it "the town where I was born - up Lantern Yard".
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #550 ch. 21: "To my old country - to the town where I was born - up Lantern Yard"; "making their way through the streets of a great manufacturing town"; "as they came to a narrow alley".

findings.claim: "Eliot's narrator describes this process using the novel's opening quotation: 'In old days there were angels ...'" Flashcards in lessons 2 and 7 call it "the opening quotation"; lesson 4 prints it as "an extract from Silas's reflections on Eppie".
findings.truth: The passage is the last paragraph of Chapter 14, well into the book, and it is the narrator's comment, not Silas's reflection. A student who writes that the novel opens with it, or that Silas thinks it, loses credit for knowledge of structure.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #550, end of ch. XIV (immediately before CHAPTER XV). The novel actually opens "In the days when the spinning-wheels hummed busily in the farmhouses ...".

findings.claim: The gold is hidden and stolen "beneath the floorboards" (lessons 2, 3 x2, 4, and a lesson 3 flashcard stem).
findings.truth: Silas keeps the coins in a hole under loose bricks in his floor, covered with sand. The bricks and the sand are load-bearing plot detail: Dunstan finds the hoard by the finger-marks in the sand, and Silas later fails to notice the disturbed sand.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #550 ch. 2: "had taken up some bricks in his floor underneath his loom ... covering the bricks with sand whenever he replaced them"; ch. 4: "inserting the thin end of the hook between the bricks, found that they were loose".

findings.claim: "Eliot uses dramatic irony here: the reader knows Dunsey is dead, but the characters do not."
findings.truth: The reverse. Eliot withholds Dunstan's death from the reader as well. Chapter 4 ends with him walking off into the dark carrying the bags, and nothing more is said until the skeleton surfaces sixteen years later in Chapter 18. There is no dramatic irony in this episode, and a structure answer built on it would be marked wrong.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #550, end of ch. IV: "So he stepped forward into the darkness." First disclosure at ch. XVIII: "there he lies - has lain for sixteen years, wedged between two great stones."

findings.claim: "He tells the parish: 'I've come to love her ... she'll be my little un.'" The same fabricated line appears in lesson 3 (content, a printed extract with mark scheme, a flashcard), lesson 6 (content, a printed extract with mark scheme, a flashcard) and lesson 7 (the memorise-these list and a flashcard) - nine places.
findings.truth: A splice of two speeches sixteen years apart. Silas says "But she'll be MY little un ... She'll be nobody else's" to Dolly Winthrop in ch. 14. "I'd come to love her" belongs to ch. 19, spoken to Godfrey Cass when he tries to claim Eppie. Neither is said to the parish. A student writing the composite in the exam would be quoting words Eliot never wrote.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #550 ch. XIV: "'But she'll be _my_ little un,' said Marner, rather hastily. 'She'll be nobody else's.'" ch. XIX: "why didn't you say so sixteen year ago, and claim her before I'd come to love her".

findings.claim: "'I think those have the least feeling that act wrong to begin with,' Eliot's narrator observes" (lesson 3), "the narrator observes" and "This is Eliot's central moral observation" (lesson 4, plus a mark scheme that rewards calling it "an authorial comment (Eliot's narrator intervening)" and a flashcard headed "Which narrator quotation"), and a lesson 7 flashcard headed "Which Eliot line".
findings.truth: The line is dialogue. Nancy Lammeter says it to Godfrey in ch. 11, before their marriage, when he asks her to encourage him to be a better man. The irony that Godfrey's own future wife delivers the novel's verdict on him is the point, and it is lost when the line is handed to the narrator.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #550 ch. XI: "'I think those have the least feeling that act wrong to begin with,' said Nancy, sending out a flash in spite of herself."

findings.claim: "moral cowardice: A deep sense of dishonour or inadequacy." (glossary entry and the matching dfn tooltip).
findings.truth: That is a definition of shame. Moral cowardice is failing to do the right thing because of what it would cost you.
findings.evidence: Internal: the definition does not describe the term it is attached to.

findings.claim: "When Eppie toddles away and falls into the stone-pit (the same pit where Dunsey drowned), Silas panics." A lesson 5 mark scheme repeats it as "Eppie nearly falls in as a toddler".
findings.truth: Eppie never goes near the Stone-pit. She cuts her linen tether with Silas's scissors and runs out of the open door; Silas fears she has fallen in and searches the pit in terror, then finds her sitting unharmed in the mud beside a pond in the next field, using her boot as a bucket.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #550 ch. XIV: "Eppie had run out by herself - had perhaps fallen into the Stone-pit ... Here, however, sat Eppie, discoursing cheerfully to her own small boot".

findings.claim: Godfrey "contributes anonymous gifts" to Eppie's upbringing.
findings.truth: The help is open, and Silas names the giver: Mr Cass built the new end of the cottage and gave them beds. Nothing in the novel is anonymous.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #550 ch. XVI: "Mr. Cass's been so good to us, and built us up the new end o' the cottage, and given us beds and things".

findings.claim: "She had offered to adopt a child years earlier, and Godfrey had refused, knowing he already had one."
findings.truth: Straight inversion. Godfrey pressed Nancy to adopt Eppie, who was then about twelve, and Nancy refused, because adopting a child after children of your own had been denied you was "to try and choose your lot in spite of Providence". Lessons 4 and 6 state the correct version, so this lesson also contradicts its own unit.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #550 ch. XVII: "Nancy's difficult resistance to her husband's wish"; "'But why should you think the child would turn out ill?' said Godfrey, in his remonstrances"; "Godfrey had from the first specified Eppie, then about twelve years old, as a child suitable for them to adopt."

findings.claim: "Nancy is hurt and angry"; "What she cannot forgive is the deception"; lesson 6: "anger at the lies, not jealousy of Molly".
findings.truth: Eliot writes the opposite. Nancy shows no anger at the confession and she does forgive Godfrey; what she feels is regret for the years the concealment wasted.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #550 ch. XVIII: "There was no indignation in her voice - only deep regret"; "The wrong to me is but little, Godfrey: you've made it up to me".

findings.claim: "He tells Eppie that the gold 'takes no hold of me now ... I've got you.'"
findings.truth: "I've got you" is invented. The real speech is "It takes no hold of me now ... the money doesn't. I wonder if it ever could again - I doubt it might, if I lost you, Eppie." The genuine wording is stronger, because Silas admits the gold could reclaim him.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #550 ch. XIX.

findings.claim: "the bonds of affection and shared experience that Silas has built over eighteen years".
findings.truth: Sixteen years. Eppie is eighteen at the end, but she arrived as a toddler and Part 2 opens sixteen years after her arrival - the number every other lesson in the unit uses.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #550 ch. XVI (sixteen-year gap); ch. XVIII: "my brother Dunstan, that we lost sight of sixteen years ago"; ch. XIX: "why didn't you say so sixteen year ago".

findings.claim: Printed extract: "... We see no white-winged angels now. But yet men are led away from threatening destruction, and even the hands of little children draw them into quiet neighbourhood." The mark scheme then analyses "Hands of little children" and "Quiet neighbourhood".
findings.truth: The second sentence is fabricated. Eliot wrote: "But yet men are led away from threatening destruction: a hand is put into theirs, which leads them forth gently towards a calm and bright land, so that they look no more backward; and the hand may be a little child's." Neither "hands of little children" nor "quiet neighbourhood" occurs anywhere in the novel, so the top-band answer rewards analysis of words that do not exist.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #550, end of ch. XIV; grep for "quiet neighbourhood" and "hands of little children" returns nothing.

findings.claim: "character arc: A character who undergoes significant internal change during the course of a narrative." (glossary entry and matching dfn tooltip).
findings.truth: An arc is the change, not the character. The lesson's own flashcard already defines it correctly.
findings.evidence: Internal: the definition contradicts flashcard 1 of the same lesson.

findings.claim: Knowledge check stem: "How many marks is each part of the Edexcel Component 2 Section A question worth?"
findings.truth: The keyed answer (20 marks each) is correct, but the stem carries a spec code and a component/section code, both banned house strings that would fail the unit validator.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT.md banned-strings list; specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md L1337-1360 confirms 20 + 20.

findings.claim: All 42 practice questions in the unit are typed "20 marks - Extract Analysis". Only 14 of them print an extract; the other 28 are whole-novel essays ("How does Eliot present the theme of community and belonging in the novel as a whole?").
findings.truth: The mark count is right, but the label is wrong for the part (b) questions, which are whole-text essays marked for AO1. The house vocabulary already has "20 marks - Whole Text Essay" and "20 marks - Wider Text Response". Two options: (a) relabel the 28 whole-text items in this unit now, or (b) hold it for a family-wide pass, because the sibling Edexcel 19th-century-novel units (jane-eyre, pride-and-prejudice, a-christmas-carol) carry exactly the same blanket label and fixing one unit alone leaves the family inconsistent. Recommendation: option (b), a single scripted relabel across the Edexcel 19th-century-novel units, since the rule (extract printed = Extract Analysis, otherwise Whole Text Essay) is mechanical.
findings.evidence: grep of scripts/_retrofc/units: 476 "20 marks - Extract Analysis" across the corpus, 99 "20 marks - Whole Text Essay", 124 "20 marks - Wider Text Response"; the three sibling Edexcel novel units use the extract label exclusively.

findings.claim: Whole Text Method step 2 says "You need 10-12 quotations", then "The five quotations in this course cover most exam questions"; the exam tip says "five strong quotations are better than fifteen vague ones".
findings.truth: Internally inconsistent revision advice in one lesson. Not a factual error about the text or the spec, so no edit; worth a tidy if the lesson is opened for any other reason.
findings.evidence: Lesson 7 content n23, n27 and exam_tip n33.

summary: No lesson is clean: all seven carry at least one finding. Two quotations are fabricated (a spliced 'I've come to love her ... she'll be my little un' that appears nine times, including the memorise-these list, and an invented second sentence on the 'white-winged angels' extract), the novel's sharpest moral line is handed to the narrator when Nancy Lammeter says it, Eppie is said to fall into the stone-pit and Dunstan's death is called dramatic irony when Eliot conceals it, the Godfrey/Nancy adoption roles are inverted, and both exam-technique lessons give part (a) and part (b) the same AO pair when the board marks (a) for AO2 alone and (b) for AO1 alone.
